Take the coat of a man who promised to cover a stranger’s debt.
Keep it as a deposit if he backs a foreign woman’s loan.

If you greet your neighbor in a loud voice at sunrise,
he will treat it as an insult.

A constant drip on a rainy day
and a wife who picks fights are the same.

Holding her back is like holding back a gale,
or like gripping oil in your right hand.{c}

Iron makes iron sharp,
and one person makes another sharp.{d}

Whoever takes care of a fig tree gets to eat its figs,
and whoever serves his master is honored.

Water shows you your face,
and a person’s heart shows who he is.

The grave and the place of ruin are never full,
and neither are human eyes.{e}

A pot tests silver, and a furnace tests gold,
and a person is tested by the praise he gets.{f}

Even if you crush a fool with a pestle in a bowl of grain,
his foolishness will not leave him.

Know how your sheep are doing.
Pay attention to your herds,

because wealth does not last forever,
and a crown is not handed down from one age to the next.

When the hay is cut and new grass shows up,
and the mountain plants are gathered,

lambs will give you clothing,
and goats will pay for a field.

There will be plenty of goat’s milk for your food,
enough to feed your whole family
and keep your servant girls alive.

notes.text: Or “deceitful,” from another way of reading the Hebrew.
The second line is uncertain. The Septuagint says, “but the soul is torn apart by troubles.”
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
Or “so a person sharpens his friend.”
The Septuagint adds, “Anyone who stares is disgusting to the Lord, and those who are not taught do not hold back their tongues.”
The Septuagint adds, “The heart of lawbreakers looks for trouble, but an honest heart looks for knowledge.”

verses.text:
The wicked flee though nobody is after them,
but the good are bold like young lions.

When a country turns against God, it has many rulers,
but with a person of understanding and knowledge, order lasts.{a}

A poor man who crushes other poor people
is like a hard rain that leaves no crops.

People who walk away from the teaching{b} applaud the wicked,
but people who hold to the teaching oppose them.

Evil people cannot grasp what is just,
but those who seek Yahweh grasp all of it.

A poor person who lives honestly is better off
than a rich person who lives two crooked lives.

A child with understanding follows the teaching,
but one who hangs around with big eaters shames his father.

Anyone who gets rich through high interest and unfair profit
is saving it up for someone kind to the poor.

If a person refuses to listen to the teaching,
even his prayers are disgusting.

Whoever leads honest people onto an evil road
will fall into his own pit,
but people without blame will receive good things.

A rich person thinks he is wise,
but a poor person with understanding sees through him.

When good people triumph, there is a great celebration.
When the wicked take over, people hide.

Whoever hides his wrongs will not succeed,
but whoever admits them and quits will find mercy.

Blessed is the person who always stays humble before God.
Whoever hardens his heart falls into trouble.

A growling lion or an attacking bear
is what a wicked ruler is to helpless people.

A leader with no understanding is a cruel oppressor,
but one who hates dishonest gain will live long.

Someone weighed down by the guilt of murder
will run until he dies. Let no one stop him.{c}

Whoever lives without blame will be kept safe,
but one who lives two crooked lives will suddenly fall.{d}

People who work their land will have plenty to eat.
People who chase empty dreams will have plenty of poverty.

A trustworthy person is richly blessed,
but someone rushing to get rich will not stay innocent.

Taking sides is not good,
yet some will do wrong for a crust of bread.

A greedy person{e} hurries to get rich
and does not realize that need is on its way.

In the end, a person who corrects others earns more thanks
than one who flatters.

Whoever steals from his father or mother and says, “That is not wrong,”
is a partner of someone who destroys.

A greedy person starts fights,
but whoever trusts Yahweh will prosper.

Whoever trusts his own mind is a fool,
but whoever lives wisely will be safe.

Whoever gives to the poor will never go without,
but whoever looks away will be cursed again and again.

When the wicked take charge, people hide.
When they die out, good people grow in number.

notes.text: The Hebrew of this verse is hard to read.
Hebrew torah. It probably means the teaching of wise people as well as God’s law. The same word is used in verses 7 and 9.
The Septuagint adds, “Correct your son, and he will love you and bring honor to your soul. He will not obey a lawless nation.”
Or “will fall into a pit,” reading one letter another way.
Literally “the man with an evil eye,” as in 23:6.

verses.text:
A person who is corrected many times and still refuses to bend
will be broken suddenly, with no way to be fixed.

When good people grow in number, the nation is glad.
When a wicked person rules, the nation groans.

Someone who loves wisdom makes his father happy,
but someone who spends time with women who sell themselves wastes his money.

A king who is fair gives his country strength,
but a man who loads on taxes{a} brings it down.

A person who flatters his neighbor
sets a trap for his own feet.

An evil person’s sin is a trap,
but a good person sings and celebrates.

A good person cares about the rights of the poor.
A wicked person does not understand them.

Mockers can set a whole city on fire,
but wise people calm anger down.

If a wise person argues in court with a fool,
the fool shouts and laughs, and nothing is settled.

Bloodthirsty people hate someone who is innocent,
and they go after the life of an honest person.{b}

A fool spills out all his anger,
but a wise person holds it in and cools it down.

When a ruler pays attention to lies,
all of his officials turn wicked.

The poor man and the bully have this in common:
Yahweh gave sight to both.

A king who judges the poor honestly
will keep his throne forever.

Correction brings wisdom,
but a child left to do whatever he wants shames his mother.

When the wicked increase, so does sin,
but good people will see them fall.

Correct your child and he will bring you peace.
He will bring joy to your soul.

Without a message from God,{c} people run wild,
but happy are those who follow the teaching.

Words alone will not correct a servant.
He understands, but he will not do it.

Do you see someone who talks without thinking?
A fool has more hope than he does.

If you pamper a servant from boyhood,
you will find in the end that he turns soft.{d}

An angry person stirs up arguments,
and a hothead sins in many ways.

A person’s pride will bring him down,
but a humble spirit will win honor.

To split loot with a thief is to hate your own life.
You hear the curse and say nothing.{e}

Fear of people is a trap,
but whoever trusts Yahweh is set up high and safe.

Many people want a meeting with the ruler,
but justice for a person comes from Yahweh.

Good people hate those who are unjust.
The wicked hate those who live honestly.

notes.text: Hebrew terumot, “contributions.” It may mean forced gifts or heavy taxes.
Or “but honest people care about his life.”
Hebrew hazon, “vision,” a message from God given to prophets.
The meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain. It may also mean “an heir” or “a cause of grief.”
A public curse was spoken against any witness who kept back what he knew (Leviticus 5:1).

verses.text:
These are the words of Agur{a} son of Jakeh, a message.{b}
The man said this to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal:{c}

I am more like a beast than a human.
I lack a person’s understanding.

Wisdom has not been taught to me,
and the Holy One is unknown to me.

Who has climbed up to heaven and come back down?
Who has caught the wind in his fists?
Who has folded the seas into a cloak?
Who has set up the far edges of the earth?
Tell me his name and his son’s name, if you know!

Every promise of God has been tested like metal in fire.
He shields all who run to him for safety.

Never add to what he has said,
or he will scold you and prove you a liar.

I ask you for two things.
Do not refuse me before I die.

Keep lies and false words far from me.
Give me neither poverty nor riches.
Just give me the food I need each day.

If I have too much, I might turn from you
and ask, “Who is Yahweh?”
If I am poor, I might become a thief
and bring shame on the name of my God.

Never accuse a servant in front of his master,
or he will curse you and you will pay.

There are those who curse their own fathers
and never speak a kind word of their mothers.

Some people think they are clean,
but they have never been washed of their dirt.

Some people look down on everyone.
How proudly they raise their eyes!

Some people have teeth like swords
and jaws like knives.
They eat the poor off the earth,
and the needy from among people.

The leech{d} has two daughters named “Give!” and “Give!”
Three things are never satisfied,
and four never say, “That is plenty!”

They are the grave, a womb with no child,
soil that always needs more rain,
and fire, which never says, “Stop!”

The eye that laughs at a father
and scorns a mother’s teaching
will be pecked out by valley ravens
and swallowed by young eagles.

Three things are too amazing for me.
Four things I cannot understand:

the path of an eagle in the sky,
the path of a snake on a rock,
the path of a ship on the open sea,
and the path of a man with a young woman.{e}

An unfaithful wife acts like this:
she finishes a meal, dabs her lips,
and says, “I have done no harm.”

Three things make the earth tremble.
It cannot carry four:

a slave who becomes king,
and a godless fool with a full stomach,

an unloved woman who finally gets a husband,
and a servant girl who takes her mistress’s place.

Four creatures on earth are tiny,
yet they are extremely wise:

Ants are not strong,
yet they store food all summer.

Rock badgers{f} have little strength,
yet they make their homes among the cliffs.

Locusts have no king,
yet they all go out in organized lines.

A lizard{g} can be caught in your hand,
yet it lives in the palaces of kings.

Three creatures walk with grand style.
Four stride proudly:

the lion, the strongest animal,
which backs down from nothing;

the proud rooster,{h} the male goat,
and a king whose army surrounds him.{i}

If you have acted like a fool and made yourself important,
or if you have plotted evil,
put your hand over your mouth.

notes.text: Agur may mean “collector” or “hired man.” Jakeh may mean “devoted” or “obedient.” Nothing more is known about either one. The Septuagint does not treat these as names. It says, “My son, respect my words and accept them,
Hebrew hamassa, “the message.” It could also be “of Massa,” a people of north Arabia who came from Ishmael (Genesis 25:14). Compare 31:1.
Ithiel means “God is with me,” and Ucal may mean “I am able.” If the Hebrew letters are divided another way, the line reads, “I am tired, God. I am tired, God, and worn out.”
Hebrew aluqah. It may be a leech that sucks blood, or a made-up monster that drinks blood.
Or “a girl.” Hebrew almah, a young woman old enough to marry.
Hebrew shephanim, the rock hyrax, a small animal that lives among rocks.
Or “spider.” The meaning of the Hebrew word semamit is uncertain.
Hebrew zarzir motnayim, literally “belted at the waist.” The animal is uncertain. The Septuagint says “a rooster walking boldly among the hens.” Others suggest a greyhound or a war horse.
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
This verse plays on the Hebrew word aph, which means both “nose” and “anger.”

subheads.21: Four Things the Earth Cannot Bear

verses.text: These are the words of King Lemuel,{a} a message{b} his mother taught him:

What should I tell you, my son? What, son I carried?
What, son I promised to God?

Do not give your strength to women,
or your life to those who destroy kings.

It is not for kings, Lemuel, to drink wine.
Kings should not do it.
Rulers should not crave beer,

or they will drink and forget the law,
and treat every poor person unfairly.

Offer beer to someone who is dying,
and wine to people who are filled with grief.

Let them drink and forget how poor they are,
and not remember their misery.

Speak for people who have no voice,
and for the rights of everyone who is helpless.{c}

Say what is right, judge with fairness,
and stand up for the poor and those in need.

Who can find a wife with strong character?{d}
Her value is much greater than jewels.

Her husband puts his full trust in her,
and he will not lack for gain.

She brings him good, never harm,
every day of her life.

She picks out wool and linen
and works with it happily.

She is like ships that carry trade goods.
She brings her food from distant lands.

She rises in the dark hours.
She feeds her household
and gives her servant girls their tasks.

She inspects a field and buys it.
With her own earnings she plants a vineyard.

She puts on strength like a belt
and makes her arms powerful.

She sees that her business does well.
Her lamp burns late into the night.

She grips the spinning stick,
and her fingers work the spindle.

She gives freely to the poor
and reaches out a hand to those in need.

She does not fear snow for her family,
because everyone at home wears warm red clothing.{e}

She makes bedspreads for her home.
She wears fine linen and purple cloth.

Her husband is well known at the city gate,
where he takes a seat with the country’s leaders.

She sews linen garments to sell.
She hands belts to the merchants.

Strength and dignity are her clothes,
and she laughs about the days ahead.

Wisdom comes out when she speaks,
and kind teaching{f} is on her tongue.

She watches over everything in her home
and never eats the bread of laziness.

Her children stand and call her blessed.
Her husband praises her too:

“Many women have done noble things,
but you have done better than every one.”

Charm fools people, and beauty fades like a breath.{g}
A woman who respects Yahweh is the one who deserves praise.

Give her the reward her hands have earned,
and let her work praise her at the city gate.

notes.text: Lemuel means “belonging to God.” He is not known from anywhere else. The Septuagint does not read a name here (see the next note).

Hebrew massa. It could also mean “king of Massa,” the north Arabian people named at 30:1. The Septuagint says, “My words were spoken by God, the answer of a king, whom his mother taught.” It also places some of 31:1–9 elsewhere.
Or “who are left alone.” Literally “children of passing away.”

Hebrew eshet chayil, a woman of strength, skill, and worth. The same phrase is used of Ruth (Ruth 3:11) and in 12:4. Verses 10–31 form an acrostic poem. Each verse starts with the next letter of the 22 Hebrew letters.
Or, following the Septuagint and some other old copies, “double clothing.”
Hebrew torat chesed, which may mean “the teaching of faithful love” or “kindly instruction.”
Hebrew hevel, “vapor” or “breath,” the key word of Ecclesiastes.
